title: a let, a var, and a binding reassigned from inside a function are all opaque layer expressions, because the initializer is not what Layer.provide will receive
notes: specification/requirements.mdx, 'Layer Algebra': 'A layer MUST associate each capability's nominal context key with a compatible service instance', and 'Satisfaction': 'When the compiler knows the complete closure, an unsatisfied capability MUST be a compile error.' The closure is a property of the layer that ARRIVES at `Layer.provide`. A mutable binding is not that layer — it is a name that may hold a different one by the time the provide runs — so the compiler does not know the closure and `SMITHERS2104` is the honest verdict. WHY THIS CASE EXISTS: a backend that resolved a layer by following a binding to its initializer certified all three of these programs. Each is initialised with a Directory layer and reassigned to a Clock one, and the body reads Directory, so the certified program compiles and then panics: the runtime registry holds Clock. That is a fail-open a corpus with only `const` layer cases cannot see, and until 2026-08-27 `SMITHERS2104` had exactly one case in the whole corpus. THE THIRD BINDING IS THE ONE THAT MATTERS. `reassignedLet` and `reassignedVar` are reassigned in the same statement list as their declaration, so a resolver that merely refuses to follow a binding with more than one assignment IN THE SAME SCOPE catches them. `reassignedInAHelper` is reassigned only from inside `swap`, so a scope-local scan sees a binding assigned exactly once at its declaration and follows it happily. The `var` spelling is here for a narrower reason: `var` is function-scoped and hoisted, so a resolver keyed on `let`/`const` declaration kinds treats it as a third case rather than as the same one. WHAT THIS CASE DELIBERATELY DOES NOT PIN: the message. `SMITHERS2104` carries a fixed sentence naming no binding and no capability, worded differently on the two backends ('this POC cannot prove' versus 'the compiler cannot prove'), so `messageContains` would freeze wording that is explicitly not the contract. It also declares no `SMITHERS2101`: an opaque layer contributes no known provided set, so there is nothing to report as unsatisfied. THE NEGATIVE DIRECTION IS NOT DUPLICATED HERE, deliberately — it already exists and is what stops this rule from degrading a precise diagnosis into an opaque one: `layer-provide-missing-a-capability` holds a `const` layer that really is missing a capability and must answer `SMITHERS2101` naming it, NOT `SMITHERS2104`, and `layer-merge-satisfies-both` holds a `const` layer that resolves and must keep RUNNING. A fix that answers 'opaque' for every binding turns both of those red rather than passing this one for the wrong reason. VERIFIED LOAD-BEARING, not assumed: mutating the THIRD declared column from 41 to 38 — the column its two siblings report, so the mutation is the answer a backend that lost the helper-reassigned binding's own position would give — turns the case red on BOTH backends with the position diff printed, and the file was restored byte-identically (sha256 482e62b643a6782c5b14c8902fc23f37fcf5b11d171edf9a6cdfdcbb1b9bbca1 before and after, that digest being this file's content at the moment the mutation ran — the sentence recording it is appended afterwards, so the shipped file necessarily hashes differently).
